entries.title: Dead End
entries.subtitle: Chapter 1
entries.summary: The sun cast uncountable shadows across the ocean, and to him they felt like the bars of a cell.
entries.intro:
The sun cast uncountable shadows across the ocean, and to him they felt like the bars of a cell.

They stretched so far it seemed they could touch the orange horizon, but it was only a trick, played by a million towers and a sinking sun. The sight should have been remarkable. One could only wonder how it looked from the other side—what the ocean saw.

He had never learned to swim. Nobody in his district had. The ocean was something you looked at from above.

He had been running for six hours. This was where the running ended.

He had come up through the tower the only way left to him: over the bridges, across the annex roofs, through shafts meant for pipes and not for people, always up, because every way down had been closed behind him. His hands were torn open. He could not remember where. All he knew was that this was the last floor. Above him there was nothing but sky.

Behind him the city never ended. Concrete, then glass, then concrete, five hundred floors and more, until the haze took it. Bridges threaded the gaps between the towers. On the face of the nearest, a screen the size of a district sold a smile to no one, and under it a family name stood in letters ten floors tall, the kind of name that was a building before it was a person.

At the edge of his sight, the chip behind his left eye drew its pale line, as it had every day since he was six. It never turned off. It had never occurred to him that it could.

Even though it wasn't dark yet, a new light flickered to life every so often.

Up here, the city was gone. No footsteps. No horns. Nothing. Only the wind, shrill and relentless. Each breath came faster, harder, and was not enough. The air was too thin.

Why bother breathing so hard?

The building swayed like a pendulum. The wind howled and clawed at him, as if it meant to take him away.

Maybe the wind will do it for me.

His legs shook, and he let them.

Behind him, nobody spoke. Nobody had spoken since the door.

He did not regret being here. He had come through the whole structure to reach this roof, and he wasn't about to gift the wind—nor them—a victory. If he was going to die, it would be with his own two hands. His choice.

Am I really that eager to die?

The thought hung there. He had come all the way up for exactly that.

Why did his feet suddenly feel so heavy?

Does anything matter anyway?

If he decided against it now, it wouldn't change anything. They were not police. Police came with sirens and papers, and ended in a cell. These had no sirens. These had no papers. What waited behind him would not look like a sentence. It would not look like anything.

His hair danced in time with the wind, his clothes barely clinging to him. He dragged his feet, never lifting them, as if the rooftop itself were the only anchor keeping him from the sky.

One step. And another. And another.

He looked back.

Seven of them, in the same grey, pressed into the lee of the access door where the wind could not reach. A small emblem was stitched at each collar. Their faces showed nothing, as if something had been poured into them and left to set. A coat snapped like a flag. No one moved. They did not step onto the gravel. The wind would have taken any of them in three paces, and they knew it.

They watched. They only had to wait.

He turned away. It cost him nothing. They were not people he could speak to.

A gust almost took him. His feet stayed planted. He inched forward against it until the roof ran out.

The edge was a low lip of concrete, no higher than his shin, slick with cold. He set his toes against it.

Beyond it, nothing. A canyon between towers, and in the canyon no bottom. Bridges, thin as threads. Screens glowing floor after floor, the same smile repeating itself down into the dark until the light simply gave up.

He had spent years learning not to fall. It was the one fear his body had never let go of.

His heartbeat scattered. His mind blurred with it. A wild exhilaration surged through him, tangled with dread.

He held his breath.

Sky.

Then not sky.

Wind in his mouth, in his eyes, in the hollow where his stomach had been. Something enormous went by: glass, a smile, a smile, a smile, too fast to be anything. His arms were somewhere. The world turned over, and he could not tell which way was down, and then he could, because it was coming.

A bridge. A light. Concrete streaming past like water.

Oh shit.

The thought arrived alone, small, and everything else in him went quiet around it.

He had jumped. He had actually jumped.

He remembered a lamp.

A low table in a kitchen too small for two. A lamp that was always on. A girl with one sock half off and a tablet glowing in her hands, who did not look up. You're late, she had said. I wasn't waiting. I was studying. Both can be true. A plate under an upturned bowl, still warm.

She'll be better off.

It was the last thing he had told himself on the way up. Only now, with nothing under him, did he hear it for what it was.

The fall went on.

Kalfu.

Her voice, from a night that was not here. Nobody else said it like that, the way you say the name of something you mean to keep.

Something clenched low in his abdomen, hard, as if a hand that had always been inside him had finally closed. Pain coiled outward, deep and old, and the whole night held its breath.

The roof was once again desolate.

entries.title: Still Water
entries.subtitle: Chapter 2
entries.intro:
Water.

It hit him from every side at once. No sky, no wall, no down. Cold in his mouth, in his eyes, in the gaps of his clothes. He kicked, and nothing pushed back. He did not know which way the air was.

He had never learned to swim.

Up. Which way is up.

There was light somewhere, a bright smear, and he went toward it with his arms and his whole body, and his lungs were on fire, and then something broke and there was air.

He coughed. His hand slapped at nothing, then at something: concrete, smooth, with a lip he could hook his fingers over. He dragged himself onto it and lay there, spitting water, shaking.

The water was clear.

That was the first thing his mind could hold. Clear as glass, down and down, and under him the towers kept going: windows, floors, bridges, sinking into blue until the blue went dark. A city, with the water already in it.

He rolled over and looked up.

It was noon.

That was wrong. He had jumped at dusk. He could still feel the orange of it on his skin. Now the sun stood small and white in a sky of perfect blue, without a single cloud, and the light fell on towers he almost knew. The same kind of concrete and glass, hundreds of floors, on every side. But clean. No stains. No cracks. The screens on the walls were blank and white.

High above the bridges, water fell across the sky in long clear ribbons, slowly, sideways, from nowhere to nowhere. Streams ran down the faces of the towers, along the seams of the concrete, floor after floor.

There was no sound. Not wind. Not machines. He heard his own coughing, barely, and the city gave nothing back.

He pressed a hand to his eye, out of habit. The chip behind it showed him nothing. No hour. No signal. No pale line at the edge of his sight that had been there since he was six. For the first time in his life, the only thing inside his head was him.

This is not the city.

Something low in his stomach was still closed, tight, a fist that had not opened. He knew what it was. Everyone knew. It was a story told in classrooms and at funerals and by drunk uncles about somebody's cousin: the well. The Shardwell. The first dive. When it woke, you went inside, and the world outside stopped for you. Wells belonged to the old families, the ones with names on the towers. Not to people like him.

It woke. It's in me. This is inside.

He said it again until it stopped sounding like a joke. Inside. Somewhere under the world, in the place the old gods had left behind when they died.

The stories said the first dive could be finished. The stories said it was made for the one who went in. They did not say what finishing was. They did not say who had made it. They said some people never finished, and were found afterward, still breathing, with no one in them.

He looked at the water. It lay quietly against the concrete an arm's length from his hand, clear and harmless.

He stood. He backed away from it. He put his hands on the wall.

Up.

It was what his body knew. A ledge, a pipe, a seam. Up was away from the water, and away from the water was the only direction that made sense.

He had been climbing for hours.

He did not know how many. The sun had not moved. That was how he knew it had been hours: he had watched it, over and over, waiting for it to lean, and it stayed exactly where it was, small and white and high, as if someone had pinned it there.

Chrona.

The word came from nowhere, from a poster on a classroom wall. Five names in a row, and a rhyme the children sang to remember them. Chrona, Vast, Nyther, Axion, Anastasis. He could not remember what any of them were for. Chrona was the one with the clocks.

Is this yours, then?

Dead gods did not do things. That was the other thing they said. So who?

The names turned over in his head like coins in a pocket, and meant nothing, and he kept climbing.

A ledge, then a pipe, then a bridge cable as thick as his waist, then another ledge. His hands were open and raw. He crossed a gap he should not have been able to cross, and did not think about it. He had stopped counting floors at three hundred. Every floor was the same. The same clean concrete, the same empty windows, the same stream of water running down the same seam. No stains. No fingerprints. A city this size should have smelled of people. It smelled of nothing.

A foothold gave. The streams had made the concrete slick, and his left foot went out from under him, and for one terrible heartbeat there was nothing under him at all. His fingers caught. His body swung. He hung over hundreds of floors with his whole weight on four torn fingers, his mouth open and no sound coming out.

He had spent years learning not to do this.

He pulled himself up. His arms shook. He did not look down. It was the only rule he had left.

At last the cable ended in a wide platform of poured concrete, flat, sheltered by a deep overhang. It stood at the edge of the tower, and here the city ended. His legs stopped on their own. He stood there with his hands hanging open and his chest working, and for the first time since the water, he was not moving.

To the east, past the last towers, lay the coast.

He knew it. It was the same ocean he had watched from the roof, the same one whose long shadows had looked like bars. It went all the way to the horizon, flat and bright, the same blue as the sky, without one wave. It did not look like the same ocean. It looked like a floor.

The city began to ring.

It started far below, a single low note, and then it was everywhere. Every pane of glass, every pipe, every seam in the concrete taking up the same pitch, until the whole city hummed like the rim of a glass. His own breath came back to him from three directions. His own heartbeat came back from the walls.

And under the hum, something else.

Water. Not falling. Moving. Something enormous turning over in its sleep.

He looked down.

The towers fell away beneath him in ledges and bridges and blank white screens, hundreds of floors, narrowing into a canyon. At the bottom of the canyon, so far down it was only a color, lay the water. Clear. Perfectly still. A single bright mirror at the bottom of the world, holding a small copy of the sky.

It had not moved. He had been climbing away from it for hours, and it had not moved. Out past the towers the ocean had not moved either.

Then the water moved.

A shiver crossed the mirror at the bottom of the canyon, from wall to wall, as if something under it had breathed in. And then it began to rise. Not like a flood, spilling and spreading. It rose whole, flat and level, climbing the towers like a floor in a lift, and every window it reached went blue, and full, and gone. Floor. Floor. Floor. Each one took it in a breath.

It climbed the tower below him. And the next one. And the next. All of them at once, a thousand windows drowning in order, and he heard nothing, because the sound was slower than the water and was still on its way.

And the ocean rose with it.

He saw it happen to the whole coast at once. The flat bright floor that ran to the horizon lifted, in one piece, slowly, and the horizon, which had been a line, began to climb the sky.

A floor a breath. Two. Four.

No.

Every child knew the old story. When the gods broke, the sea came back. It came once, and drowned the world, and the people who lived afterward called it the First Drowning because they were afraid there would be a second.

This is the second.

The canyon was gone. The city was disappearing from the bottom up, as though someone were erasing it.

His fingers closed on the edge of the platform. The torn skin split. He did not feel it.

The roar arrived.

It hit him from below, from everywhere, the sound of an entire city and an entire ocean being lifted, and the platform shook under his feet. The water was climbing the tower beside him now, close enough to see the foam, a hundred floors beneath him and rising.

He ran.

He went up the cable, the wall, whatever the structure gave him. He did not stop again. He did not look down again. He did not need to. It was the only sound in the world, and it was behind him.

Far above, past the last bridge, a single door stood in the face of a tower. It was lit from the inside.

It was the only thing in the whole bright city that cast a shadow.
